summary: Prince Philip briefly visited the Queen's study, spoke a dry word in account/apology, and departed for morning errands.
The Queen made a brief pencil note at the bottom of a dispatch and folded it, securing it for return.
The press liaison reviewed cuttings and filed a clipping into a file labelled 'Windsor'.
The royal chauffeur prepared a pair of limousines in the yard: polishing chrome and waiting with cars stationary and ready.
The lady-in-waiting prepared the Queen's day attire, laying out gloves, a starched blouse and a blue day dress.
Stables activity: smells of hay and warm horse, harnesses checked, and general preparation for the day's needs.
River quay scene: the Thames warm with lazy ripples, willows leaning, a motor launch drifting and tourists watching the castle.
The publicist moved through the high street, monitoring the actress's presence and adjusting plans.
A famous actress is present in town and is staying at the Castle View hotel (unnamed in this scene).
Arrival at the Hotel Castle View: limousine pulled under the shallow canopy; chauffeur opened the rear door; porters handled luggage.
Actress's arrival manner: steps out with hat low, gloves, sunglasses lifted for the doorway, turning the hotel into a stage.
Driver handled the suitcases with valet-like manner and did not loiter.
Publicist purchased the local paper at the newsagent and arranged discretely for it to be tucked away rather than displayed.
Actress inspected the silver cigarette case, noted a hairline scratch and found an arrival note slipped between the cigarettes.
Publicist gave explicit instructions about appearances and photography: no interviews in morning, meet mayor after tea, no balcony photos.
Confidante made a wry observation about costume and roofline, offering companionship and perspective.
Actress looked from the suite window at Windsor and mapped the town for publicity and image decisions.
Footman announced lunch service and later delivered a card; the actress read the single word on the name-plate.
Tom Harris sweeping outside Harris & Sons and observing the high street rhythms.
Publicist in Langley’s Newsagents signals the newsman and has a paper slipped behind the counter; press cuttings are visible in the window.
Actress's driver and the royal chauffeur pass each other in the street, exchanging professional courtesies while limousines idle in the castle yard.
Tourists cluster at the quay end of the street with cameras; local scenes of everyday life continue.
Tom tips his hat to the driver as a bellboy wheels a case; Tom comments 'Looks the part, don’t she' and receives a smile from the woman at the tea-room.
High street maintains its rhythm of commerce and observation; noticeboard and press cuttings act as public ledger of reputation.
Tom Harris observes the high street from Harris & Sons, noting local gestures of town life and the pile of press cuttings in the newsagent window.
Publicist signals the newsman; a paper is slipped behind the counter and press cuttings shown in the newsagent window.
Actress's driver and royal chauffeur pass in the street, exchanging professional courtesies while limousines idle in the castle yard.
Tourists cluster at the quay end of the street with cameras.
Tom tips his hat to the driver as a bellboy wheels a case; Tom comments that the actress 'looks the part' and receives a smile from the tea-room woman.
Royal butler shows the palace press liaison into the press office and leaves the door half-ajar.
The palace press liaison untied the string on the file labelled 'Windsor', spread the clippings and reviewed a gossip column, a thumbed photograph, and a wire story from a provincial correspondent.

The lady-in-waiting arrives; they discuss options for managing the actress's publicity including a controlled photograph, a short caption, a single wire, and escalation to the Private Secretary if anything official is billed.
Press liaison writes the options on a small memo, folds it and says he will call Miss Cavendish’s publicist and inquire with Buckingham about an official line.
Liaison replaces newspapers in the file labelled 'Windsor', reties the brown string and plans to keep the file locked until a decision is made.
The palace press liaison leaves with the file under his arm; at the threshold he hesitates and remarks they had a similar brief case once at an investiture.
